R9667.summary: Clear letter with cipher runs on the Pope's servants and the benefices the Pope wants for them; CSP Spain ii no. 548 abstracts it from a lost contemporary decipherment (the Pope has not yet declared his alliance, the French have lost hope, Theodorico was most suspected). Only fragments of the cipher runs are deciphered; the 'Claro' leaf beside it is the Abbot of Nájera's clear of 2 May 1523, not Hurtado's.

R9683.summary: The Duke of Sessa's letters report the Pope's good will after the arrest of Cardinal Soderini of Volterra; the Emperor should restore the benefices of the chamberlain Pedro and Francisco and pay the Pope what is owed him. Most of the cipher passages are not deciphered.

R9695.summary: The Pope was pleased with the Emperor's letter; the rumoured poisoning could not be verified, the Pope guards his person and eats apart, and Hurtado asks for naturalisations for the Pope's intimates (Pedro de Roma, Francisco, Theodorico). The clear text is transcribed in part; the cipher lines are not deciphered.

R9846.summary: The Pope is glad of the coming of Monsieur de Beaurain; on the contribution, money is short and every help is needed; the Pope wants France ruined or a truce (CSP Spain ii no. 617). The first third is deciphered by aligning the cipher with the clerk's clear on f. 133r; the rest of the clear (f. 133v) is not imaged.
R9846.en:
The Pope has been pleased by the news of the coming of Monsieur de Beaurain. He awaits him eagerly; his coming here at
this juncture will be useful for all business in general, and in particular for the matter of the contribution, for, as
there is little money, every help is needed, until we see whether the viceroy's going out makes the French withdraw,
for where they now are makes one think what is to come. However, the Pope's resolve is that they should go out of Italy,
and if he saw the means to humble the pride of the King of France and to aggrandise Your Majesty, His Holiness has told
me he would like to help in it.

R9866.summary: To Gattinara: Beaurain's coming was timely; the French mean, by craft or force, to stay on this side of the Alps, and the Emperor must not lose the world's respect while he spends so much on the war; Hurtado asks Gattinara's help to be paid what he is owed. Read a quarter to a third.
R9866.en:
Most Illustrious Lord,

The coming of Monsieur de Beaurain has been very timely. I have briefed him on matters here as best I understand them,
as Your Lordship will see by his letters; and since the third party in everything is negotiating here, I shall be brief.

The French want, by craft or by force, to stay on this side of the mountains, given the credit that [?they have]
[?levelled], by not having been harmed in those parts by the armies of Your Majesty, and that it is lost by being
unable to do anything. If His Majesty can, in [?no other] way does it suit him [to grant], for few or […] days, peace
or truce, if the French stay here with […] a foot of [?ground], for it will be, fearing the [?Swiss] and the
[?reputation] they have gained, [?to be], when they [?wish], lords of Italy; and that His Majesty should not be [lord]
of the world, with them leaving it.

R9867.summary: Wholly in cipher: Monsieur de Beaurain has left the Pope content with what he said on the Emperor's behalf; the Emperor must not show need of money, little can be raised; mention of the archbishop [of Capua] and the French in Italy; the writer asks for what is owed to him.

R9868.summary: Hurtado sends Gattinara a copy of his 11 March letter: the archbishop of Capua has left and all business hangs on the Datary [Giberti], who must be satisfied; benefices shared among the Cardinals; the Pope's servants should be rewarded and many Cardinals want to be Protector.
R9868.en:
Most Illustrious Lord,

By the letter that goes with this, which is a copy of the one I wrote to His Majesty on the 11th of this month, Your
Lordship will have learnt of the departure of the lord archbishop of Capua. With his absence all business has come to
hang on the Datary, and he stands as far forward with the Pope as can be. I have written to His Majesty in other letters
of the need there is to [?reward] him, because he was ill-content with the past, given the place he holds. I
hold it to be inexpedient, and every day it seems to me more necessary to [?satisfy] him. Let it not be in the
ten moneys that the Pope held on the […] of […], because he would not take them from them, for they have been shared
out among the Cardinals like the other benefices; and he thinks His Majesty will approve, as the King of France has done
with the benefices he held in France.

R9869.summary: The money the Pope offered through Beaurain; Florence has taken no decision; Cardinal Cortona and Ippolito de' Medici leave for Florence; the archbishop of Capua should be well received by the Emperor; the Pope's goodwill and words could not be better. The rest (Easter news, Hungary and the Turk, the Infante) is in clear.
R9869.en:
S[acred] C[atholic] C[aesarean] M[ajes]ty

[…] of the money that the Pope offered to Monsieur de [?Beaurain], he has [?sent] […]; the [?four] of these took […].
His Holiness has told me that he will fulfil the rest; […] but he speaks of his need.

From Florence no resolution has been taken so far; they still [?make] excuses. They say that next week Cardinal
Cortona will leave for there with Ippolito, His Holiness's nephew, and that once [there] […] [?good].

The news that they had from these parts and from England had changed everyone's purpose. Now, holding it for certain
that the French have lost Fuenterrabía, having the news by reports from Monsieur de Bourbon and from Lyon, although they
differ: some say by assault and others by terms. The French acknowledge that it is lost, but say it was by treason. It
has greatly favoured Your Majesty's affairs.

snip.cap: RAH Salazar A-30 f. 130r (R9846), Lope Hurtado to Charles V, 5 February 1524: the clear opening on Beaurain’s coming, then the cipher from para lo de con[tribucion]
snip.credit: Real Academia de la Historia, via DECODE R9846

system: Three-letter consonant-vowel-consonant nomenclator codes mixed inline with clear Spanish, with homophones at code level (ta and tu both = 'no'), codes used for syllables as well as whole words, and long words spelled letter by letter between the codes.
